chunks: And from him, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abu Basir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him about a woman who fell ill in Ramadan and died in the month of Shawwal, and she instructed me to make up the fasts on her behalf. He said: 'Did she recover from her illness?' I said: 'No, she died while still ill.' He said: 'The fasts are not made up on her behalf, for Allah did not make it obligatory upon her.' I said: 'But I wish to make up the fasts on her behalf, and she instructed me to do so.' He said: 'How can you make up something that Allah did not make obligatory upon her? If you wish to fast for your own sake, then fast.'

key_terms.لَمْ يَجْعَلْهُ عَلَيْهَا: Did not make it obligatory upon her

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on making up the fasts of a woman who died in Ramadan while still ill?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the distinction between obligatory make-up fasts (*qada*) and voluntary fasting (*nafl*) for the deceased, emphasizing that illness exempts one from the divine obligation. The Imam (peace be upon him) instructs that since the duty was not incumbent upon her during her illness, no debt is owed, yet one may still fast voluntarily to gain spiritual reward. This ruling underscores the Shia principle that *qada* is strictly for fulfilled obligations, while voluntary acts remain a personal choice for the living.
